title: You Got Served
full_review:
High-energy dance scenes will keep a young audience's toes tapping in the slight hip-hop musical "You Got Served" (Screen Gems), but the boilerplate script and shoddy direction may have them shimmying for the theater door.

Having nothing to do with subpoenas, the term "you got served" is actually slang for showing someone up or getting the best of them, which is exactly what the film's dance groups try to do to one another at neighborhood dance battles. The best of these dance crews is led by boyhood friends David (Omari Grandberry) and Elgin (Marques Houston). But naturally, as the conventional script would have it, the friends have a falling out -- over a girl and a missed rendezvous -- and end up competing against each other in the biggest dance competition of the year.

The girl is Elgin's sister (Jennifer Freeman), to whom David has taken a liking, which makes him miss Elgin's calls for help during a dangerous drop-off of goods for a local mobster (Michael Taliferro). (Elgin and David are reluctantly involved in these apparent drug deliveries and, though it's never made clear, it is implied the goods they transport are drugs.) Elgin lands in the hospital with a wrecked leg and a bad case of the grudges.

Suspense and tension are words missing from writer-director Christopher B. Stokes' vocabulary. However, one-dimensional characterizations, silly plot threads and musical cliches are firmly implanted on his word list. This is not to say, though, that the hyperchoreographed dance scenes don't have a certain bouncy, lively aspect that lends a hand in saving the film from grinding to a complete halt.

Stokes, manager of the boy band B2K, wrote the film as a vehicle for group member Grandberry, who recently left the band, and Grandberry does have a good dose of screen appeal and presence. The problem is that interest wanes as soon as the dancing stops, which means "You Got Served" holds more interest as a music video than a movie. Stokes throws in a drug thug, a nasty beating, an off-screen drive-by shooting and some very white kids from the other side of town as the main characters' big competition. But even with all this faux gritty drama mixed in with competitive street dancing, Stokes steps on his own feet and falls flat.

Yet, there is an underlying wholesomeness to this film that is refreshing. Their dance crew preaches "no cussing, no fighting and no hustling." The romance between Elgin's sister and David develops over milkshakes and culminates with a few kisses -- not a bedroom scene. Steve Harvey, as a neighborhood good guy and the film's main adult character, is not made out to be a fool, and actually offers some worthwhile advice.

The acrobatic dance moves have the teen characters jumping, gyrating, and performing gravity-defying steps that impress. One-handed handstands and head spins are par for the course, as are slow-motion strides that cause the viewer to wonder if it's the film, or are these kids their own special effect? But, unfortunately, neither the high-energy dancing nor superstar Lil' Kim's appearance at film's end can elevate "You Got Served" into anything more than mildly entertaining fare.

Because of a few crude dance moves, minor drug content, brief violence and some crass words, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
